summary:
Jamaica criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. The Offences Against the Person Act punishes buggery with up to 10 years' hard labour, and the US State Department's 2023 country report confirms the provision remains in force. No law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and individuals are not legally permitted to register a change of gender, so a trans visitor has no domestic legal recognition to rely on.

The defining case is Dwayne Jones, a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old beaten, stabbed and shot to death by a mob at a street party in 2013 after being outed. Police did not investigate the killing. The case is now before the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights as Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica, and an amicus brief filed in February 2024 argues that continued criminalisation and systemic discrimination leave transgender Jamaicans exposed to housing, educational and employment insecurity.

Police protection is unreliable. The US Department of Justice country packet records that LGBT victims do not report attacks because police leak incident details, fail to investigate violence including murder, and do not intervene during attacks. The Inter-American Commission's 2012 report on Jamaica describes the violent persecution and fear to which gay and lesbian people are subject as deplorable. Human Rights Watch documented police harassment of gay men and of HIV/AIDS outreach workers alongside community and family violence carried out with impunity and official indifference. Amnesty International's 4 June 2006 urgent appeal reported police ill-treatment and torture of LGBT people as well as vigilante attacks.

Vigilante violence remains a live risk. Amnesty documented gay men and lesbians beaten, cut, burned, raped and shot once their orientation became known, and lesbians raped and driven into exile abroad. Community members report that beatings and stonings of trans people are common but rarely reported because reporting achieves nothing.

Detention carries a specific and documented danger. The State Department reports that prisoner-on-prisoner violence is common, including severe violence against prisoners targeted for perceived LGBTQI+ identity, in facilities operating far beyond capacity; a January 2023 video showed an inmate at a pretrial police lockup beaten and attacked with scalding liquid by other inmates accusing him of being gay. No gender-recognition framework exists to inform how a trans detainee would be housed.
tangentialFactors:
The Inter-American Commission's report of 10 August 2012 places LGBT persecution inside a wider pattern of citizen security failures in Jamaica, covering police killings including the May 2010 operation and the administration of justice, with input from Jamaicans for Justice and the Jamaica Forum for Lesbians, All-Sexuals and Gays.

Human Rights Watch's documentation was launched in Kingston on 16 November 2004 with the backing of five Jamaican human-rights organisations, and the Inter-American Commission likewise drew on local civil society, indicating an established domestic advocacy infrastructure that a visitor may encounter as a source of assistance.

Amnesty International's 2006 urgent appeal also raised concern that prominent Jamaican musicians promote homophobia, a cultural influence that operates alongside the legal regime rather than within it.

The UNDP national survey published in March 2023 supplies quantified baseline data on violence and service exclusion among LGBT Jamaicans, against which the older qualitative accounts can be read.
localsOnly:
UNDP's 'Being LGBT in Jamaica' national survey of March 2023 contains dedicated chapters on violence due to prejudice and discrimination and on transgender access to health care, quantifying lived experience of violence and service exclusion under the criminalisation backdrop.

A study by University of the West Indies lecturer Carla Moore, fielded April to November 2018 and published on 5 February 2019, found that Jamaicans perceived as gay, bisexual or transgender are isolated within the penal institutions and that rehabilitation opportunities for them are basically non-existent. Movement inside facilities is severely curtailed and access to resources limited because other prisoners refuse to touch objects or sit on seats used by gay prisoners. The study estimated that about 300 of the 1,800 prisoners at Tower Street Adult Correctional Centre belong to sexual or gender minorities, reported that lesbians face prevalent corrective rape, and documented no specialised housing policy for such prisoners.

The amicus brief filed in February 2024 in Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica sets out housing insecurity, educational insecurity and employment insecurity for transgender Jamaicans under the discrimination regime.

The State Department reports correctional facilities significantly overcrowded, with Tower Street maximum-security cells at three times capacity and conditions described as harsh and life-threatening.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the inventory does not state whether the Inter-American Commission has decided Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica or what remedies, if any, it has ordered.

Unresolved: no source here gives conviction or enforcement figures for the buggery provision in recent years. The sources establish that the offence is on the books; how often it is applied is not sourced.

Unresolved: treatment of trans travellers at entry, including visa and border screening, acceptance of foreign documents bearing a changed gender marker, and any risk of being screened or questioned on gender identity, is not covered by this inventory.

Unresolved: whether conditions differ in tourist areas such as Montego Bay, Negril or Ocho Rios is not sourced in this inventory.

Currency caveat: the Amnesty appeal dates from 2006, the Human Rights Watch letter from 2004, the Inter-American Commission report from 2012 and the Department of Justice packet from 2013; whether each specific account still describes current practice is not verified here. The State Department report (2023) and the UNDP survey (March 2023) are the most recent sources.

Scope caveat: the prison study rests on 2018 fieldwork at a single facility, so its figures should not be read as a national prison-wide measurement.
